title: Largest multiplicative part of a commutative affine group and scalar extension
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. A group is of multiplicative type if over an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] it admits a closed subgroup inclusion into $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some $r\geq0$ [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type, def-sc-gm-ga]. Unipotent means admitting a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into some $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. Let $C$ be commutative. There is a largest subgroup $C_s\subseteq C$ of multiplicative type, meaning that every closed subgroup of $C$ of multiplicative type is contained in $C_s$. The represented fppf quotient $C/C_s$ is unipotent. The fppf quotient here is the sheafification of $A\mapsto C(A)/C_s(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]. For every field extension $K/k$, scalar extension gives $(C_s)_K=(C_K)_s$ as closed subgroup schemes of $C_K$. No smoothness, connectedness or perfectness is assumed.

proof.text: Write $C=\operatorname{Spec}B$. By [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra] and [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], $B$ is Noetherian: a field is Noetherian since its only ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$. Let $\mathcal H$ be the set of closed subgroups $H\subseteq C$ for which $C/H$ is unipotent; the quotients exist by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], since $C$ is commutative. The set is nonempty, containing $C$. If $I_H\subseteq B$ is the ideal of $H$, the sum $I=\sum_{H\in\mathcal H}I_H$ is finitely generated [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Each of its finitely many generators is a finite sum from the $I_H$, so $I=I_{H_1}+\cdots+I_{H_r}$ for finitely many $H_i\in\mathcal H$. Their fibre-product intersection $S$ is the closed subgroup defined by $I$: maps $B\to A$ kill $I$ exactly when they kill all $I_H$. Thus $S=\bigcap_{H\in\mathcal H}H$ scheme-theoretically, not just on field-valued points.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(a), printed p.328, and Note 16.17, printed p.329.

proof.text: The diagonal homomorphism $C\to\prod_{i=1}^r C/H_i$ has kernel $S$ on every algebra. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] its quotient by that kernel is a closed subgroup of the product. The quotient universal property [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal] identifies it with $C/S$. Choose closed immersions $C/H_i\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n_i,k}$. Block diagonal matrices give a closed immersion of their product into $\mathcal U_{\sum n_i,k}$: the coordinate map is surjective, with all off-block coordinates sent to zero. Hence $C/S$ is unipotent. In the empty-product case it is trivial and embeds in $\mathcal U_{1,k}$. By construction $S$ is contained in every closed subgroup whose quotient is unipotent.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(a), printed p.328, and Note 16.17, printed p.329.

proof.text: Let $\varphi:S\to\mathbf G_a$ be a homomorphism, and put $N=\ker\varphi$. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization], $S/N$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_a$. The map $a\mapsto\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ identifies $\mathbf G_a$ with $\mathcal U_{2,k}$, so $S/N$ is unipotent. The subgroup correspondence [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] gives an exact represented fppf sequence $1\to S/N\to C/N\to C/S\to1$. Apply [lem-sfb-unitriangular-extension]: both end groups have the required unitriangular embeddings, so $C/N$ is unipotent. The minimality in step 2 forces $S\subseteq N$, while $N\subseteq S$. Thus $\varphi=0$.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(a), printed p.328, and Note 16.17, printed p.329.

proof.text: This vanishing remains true over any field extension $L/k$. Indeed, for $A=k[S]$, [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] and [def-sc-gm-ga] identify $\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathbf G_a)$ with the primitive subspace $P(A)=\{a:\Delta a=a\otimes1+1\otimes a\}$. For a primitive element $x\in L\otimes_k A$, choose an expression $x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\otimes a_i$ with the $\lambda_i$ linearly independent over $k$. Its primitive equation is $\sum_i\lambda_i\otimes(\Delta a_i-a_i\otimes1-1\otimes a_i)=0$. Applying the coordinate functionals on the span of the $\lambda_i$ (extended to $L$ by a vector-space basis) makes every $a_i$ primitive. Since $P(A)=0$ by step 3, $x=0$. Conversely zero maps stay zero. The affine fibre-product formula identifies this Hopf algebra with $L[S_L]$.

source.place: Theorem 12.18, first paragraph of proof, printed p.237: primitive elements and linear base change.

proof.text: Apply step 4 with $L=\bar k$. The group $S_{\bar k}$ is commutative and has no nonzero additive homomorphisms. Therefore [lem-sfb-multiplicative-additive-vanishing-criterion] makes it $D_{\bar k}(M)$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$. Choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$ of $M$. The algebra map $\bar k[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_t^{\pm1}]\to\bar k[M]$, $z_i\mapsto e_{m_i}$, is surjective and respects all Hopf operations. Its spectrum is a closed group immersion into $\mathbf G_m^t$. Thus $S$ is of multiplicative type in exactly the definition of the item.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(a), printed p.328, and Note 16.17, printed p.329.

proof.text: If $H\subseteq C$ is of multiplicative type, then $H_{\bar k}$ is a closed subgroup of a split torus. By [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] it is diagonalizable. The closed unitriangular immersion of $(C/S)_{\bar k}$ is obtained by tensoring the coordinate surjection of step 2. Consequently [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial] makes the composite $H_{\bar k}\to(C/S)_{\bar k}$ trivial. It is already trivial over $k$: the difference of its coordinate map and the identity-valued coordinate map becomes zero after tensoring with $\bar k$, and $V\to\bar k\otimes_k V$ is injective for every $k$-vector space $V$ (extend a nonzero vector to a basis). Since $\ker(C\to C/S)=S$, the inclusion of $H$ factors through $S$. Thus $C_s:=S$ is the largest multiplicative-type subgroup and has the asserted represented unipotent quotient.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(a), printed p.328, and Note 16.17, printed p.329.

proof.text: Let $K/k$ be any field extension. Applying steps 1–6 over $K$ gives $T=(C_K)_s$ with unipotent quotient. Step 4 gives $\operatorname{Hom}(S_K,\mathbf G_{a,K})=0$, hence also this vanishing over an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $K$. The criterion and the explicit generator map of step 5 make $S_K$ multiplicative, so maximality gives $S_K\subseteq T$. Quotient base change [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identifies $C_K/S_K=(C/S)_K$. This group is unipotent over $K$: tensoring with $K$ the surjective coordinate map $k[\mathcal U_{n,k}]=k[x_{ij}:i<j]\to k[C/S]$ of step 2 gives a surjection $K[x_{ij}:i<j]\to K\otimes_kk[C/S]$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] compatible with the Hopf maps, i.e. a closed group immersion $(C/S)_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,K}$, exactly as over $\bar k$ in step 6. Over $\Omega$, [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] and [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial] make $T_\Omega\to(C_K/S_K)_\Omega$ trivial. The same coordinate-basis injectivity argument of step 6 descends this equality to $K$, giving $T\subseteq S_K$. The two inclusions are inclusions of the actual closed subgroup functors in $C_K$, so $S_K=T$ as closed subgroup schemes.
